title: Nationalise the Labour, Labourise the Industry, Industrialise the Nation
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The three-line motto of BMS, line by line.
body:
Every BMS meeting ends with the same three lines, and every karyakarta knows them by heart: "Nationalise the Labour, Labourise the Industry, Industrialise the Nation." In the 1950s, when socialism and communism were the fashionable words, this motto was an unconventional idea. Today it still appears on BMS material, and its Hindi form, *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Shramik hit*, is printed on the organisation's website. This post explains what the three lines say, how they connect, and why BMS considers them a complete view of trade unionism.

## Where the motto comes from

The motto is attributed to the thinking of Dattopant Thengadi and was part of BMS's identity from its early years. It appears alongside other slogans that BMS adopted to give the labour movement a different vocabulary. According to BMS's own history, the organisation set out to be nationalist and constructive rather than merely agitational, and to treat industrial peace and production as conditions for progress.

The idea behind it is linked to the philosophy of Integral Humanism, which BMS's website credits to Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay, and to the rejection of the Marxist theory of class struggle. BMS says its fight is against injustice and exploitation, not against any class. A motto that begins with the nation and ends with the nation fits that outlook.

## Nationalise the Labour

The first line is the one most often misunderstood, because "nationalise" in ordinary speech means that the State takes over an industry. In BMS's usage, the object is the labour, not the industry. The line is generally explained as saying that the worker is first and foremost a member of the nation, and that labour is a part of the national family and not a separate class with a separate loyalty. The worker's identity is that of a citizen with a stake in the country's progress.

This is why BMS has promoted national symbols in the labour movement. Its own account says that "Bharat Mata Ki Jai" was a slogan unfamiliar in the labour field before BMS introduced it. The first line of the motto gives that practice a reason: if labour is part of the nation, labour's cause is the nation's cause.

## Labourise the Industry

The second line turns to industry. Industry exists because of labour, and BMS asks that labour be treated accordingly. In plain terms, the line says that workers should be seen as partners in an industry and not merely as hired hands. BMS's website says it favours workers' participation in industry, tied to duties as well as rights, and it speaks of an "industrial family" in which workers, management and consumers share a common interest.

It also proposes more than one pattern of ownership instead of choosing only between nationalisation and private ownership. It names cooperative, municipal and joint ownership among the options, and it says State control should be limited to sectors such as defence. The Constitution itself contains a related direction: Article 43A, added in 1976, asks the State to take steps to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings. BMS has often asked that the direction be given practical effect.

## Industrialise the Nation

The third line looks outward. A nation grows when industries grow, when production rises and when jobs are created. For BMS, trade unionism is not only about wages. It is also about **building**: production, productivity and employment.

This is visible in BMS's economic positions. Its website says it favours productivity and public accountability. It encourages the idea of producing the maximum and consuming with restraint. It also gives importance to the self-employed and to artisans, whom it calls the Vishwakarma sector, and it asks for a separate government department to support them. Those who followed the BMS's pre-budget submissions will recognise the same thinking in its requests for support to rural and micro industries, which create jobs where people live.

## One idea, three directions

Read together, the three lines form a cycle. A nationally minded worker; an industry that respects its workers; and a nation that grows strong through industry. Each line supports the next and is supported by it. If one is missing, the cycle breaks: workers who feel no belonging to the nation have little reason to protect production; an industry that ignores its workers will not be productive; and a nation without industry cannot give its workers a livelihood.

It is the practical form of BMS's wider formula, *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Mazdoor hit*, which places the interests of the nation, the industry and the worker together. A separate post in this series looks at that formula and the order of its three parts.

## A companion slogan on wages and work

Another BMS line, which is often heard at rallies, shows the same balance of duty and right. It can be translated as: we will work in the country's interest, and we will take full wages for our work. The slogan makes a claim and accepts a duty in one breath. It asks for a fair price for labour, and it commits the worker to good work. That combination is typical of the way BMS frames its demands, and it is also why the organisation describes its tradition as one of *tyag, tapasya aur balidan*, meaning sacrifice, penance and martyrdom.

## How the motto shapes practice

A motto is useful only if it changes behaviour. Three examples show how this one does.

- **Methods:** BMS says strikes should be a last resort after talks, negotiation and arbitration, and that violence should have no place. Demands are firm, but the method is meant to be constructive.
- **Policy positions:** BMS speaks for micro and small industries, for workers' participation and for tripartite consultation, which follow from the second and third lines.
- **Culture:** The organisation celebrates Vishwakarma Day as National Labour Day, in place of the more common 1 May observance, and its flag and symbols reflect the same effort to speak in an Indian idiom.

## Reading the motto critically

Whether one agrees with every application of the motto or not, it explains why BMS tends to combine firm demands with constructive methods. Critics from other labour traditions argue that a national framing can blunt conflict between employers and workers, while BMS replies that conflict is not the only way to secure justice. A reader who wishes to form an independent view would do well to read BMS's own documents, such as its policy memoranda to the National Labour Commission, and the positions of its critics, and to compare them with what actually happens at the workplace.
